newsitem.title: UK: Copper up, gold down in mixed start to 1997.
newsitem.headline: Copper up, gold down in mixed start to 1997.

text.p: Speculators used thin trading conditions on Thursday to push world copper prices higher, while on the precious metals market gold slumped to its lowest level for over three years.
On the soft commodity markets the trend was also mixed, with cocoa gaining ground while coffee and sugar slipped.
Across the board exchanges were hit by the post-new year trading lull.
Benchmark three month copper futures finished the first trading day of 1997 at $2,167 a tonne, up $40 from Tuesday morning, the last time the market was open.
Traders expected to see the rally continue if copper can climb above $2,175, a level which it has failed to overcome on a number of occasions in recent weeks.
Friday's stock report could be the deciding factor, with a small increase in inventories already factored into the market, traders said.
Most other industrial metals took their lead from the flagship copper contract except tin, which edged lower on Far Eastern selling.
Lead was bolstered by news late in the day that a large smelter in Nordenham, Germany, had stopped production late in December until the last week of January for technical adjustments and repairs.

The plant is one of the major lead suppliers to European vehicle battery manufacturers. The disruption coincides with the peak demand season for car batteries, strengthened this winter by freezing conditions across the continent.

Gold slumped to fix at $366.55 an ounce from $367.80 in the morning. Dealers said New York selling sparked the move, noting U.S.-based investment funds still anticipated weakness in gold and any further falls would play into their hands.
Cocoa prices rallied as sterling weakened slightly against the dollar. March 1997 futures rose 15 stg to 905 stg a tonne.
Coffee and sugar both edged lower in London in sluggish trade while wheat futures in Chicago edged higher.
